title: A cold air mass that stayed, not ocean mixing memory, explains why storm cold wakes on the US East shelf lasted 30 days while Gulf of Mexico wakes recovered (55 NDBC buoys, 1982-2024)
abstract: An earlier campaign study found that 30 days after a tropical storm passes within 200 km of a NOAA buoy, sea-surface temperature (SST) on the US East shelf stays 0.44 C below no-storm years, while Gulf of Mexico SST recovers. We tested why, with the same 534 events (1982-2024) and the same placebo design (same station and calendar dates in no-storm years). We added buoy air temperature, dew point and wind, bulk heat fluxes, a WOA23 cooling potential for shelf stratification, and NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 850 hPa temperature and 500 hPa height. At days 26-34 the shelf air excess was -0.80 C (95% storm-bootstrap interval -1.15 to -0.45), larger than the SST excess (-0.46 C). Air minus sea was -0.28 C (-0.54 to -0.05), so the sea gave extra heat to the air; a cold sea that cools the air gives the opposite sign. In an event regression, the day-30 air excess removed all of the shelf-minus-Gulf SST contrast (fraction 1.00, 0.60 to 2.39). The cooling potential predicted peak cooling but removed only 0.17 (-0.16 to 0.50) of the day-30 contrast; water depth and season removed none. Reanalysis showed a 30-day trough over north-eastern North America after shelf storms (T850 -0.74 C, Z500 -16 m at days 26-34; Gulf near zero). Thus storm-linked cold weather, not ocean memory, mainly explains the slow shelf recovery. Limits: we do not show whether the storm makes the trough or the trough steers the storm; no sub-surface profiles; coarse reanalysis removed only 37-49% of the contrast; the contrast is not clear in 2011-2024.

display.caption: Placebo-corrected SST, buoy air temperature and turbulent heat-loss excess after storm passage within 200 km (clean60 events). On the US East shelf the air stays colder than the sea for 60 days and the sea keeps losing extra heat; in the Gulf of Mexico both temperatures recover and the sea loses less heat than normal.

Left: per-event day 26-34 SST excess against air excess; both regions follow one relation and differ only in their air excess. Right: fraction of the shelf-minus-Gulf day-30 SST contrast that each covariate removes (storm-bootstrap 95% intervals).

NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 composite excess of 500 hPa height and 850 hPa temperature, days 1-30 after closest approach. Shelf events come with a trough and cold air over north-eastern North America and a ridge over the western United States; Gulf events show no such pattern near the buoys.
